To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) academic staff perceive that written feedback on students’ written work is an important tool in the process of assessment and learning; (2) academic staff perceive the role of feedback to be primarily to improve the students’ writing, but also to provide a basis for the students’ future development; (3) academic staff perceive written feedback as a complex process which requires a number of different skills and abilities; (4) academic staff perceive their own feedback to be more effective than that of their colleagues
academic staff value feedback on student writing, but they also perceive it as time consuming and as a burden.
academic staff perceive written feedback on students’ written work to be important for disciplinary teaching, learning, assessment and student support.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of academic writing teachers, the nature of academic writing, the role of writing in disciplinary learning and the relationship between writing and feedback.
the question: how do teachers perceive the role of written feedback in the learning process and how do they perceive the role of academic writing teachers?
the role of written feedback on students’ writing in the context of higher education in the United Kingdom.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
academic writing teachers need to be aware of the different roles and functions of written feedback in the different contexts in which they operate.
academic staff perceptions of the role of written feedback on students’ writing are varied and complex.
academic staff in higher education institutions are not clear about the role of written feedback in the teaching and learning process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the findings indicate the need for more explicit attention to be paid to the role and utility of feedback on written work in disciplinary teaching and learning.
we have shown that written feedback on students’ written work is a complex phenomenon, which is affected by a range of contextual factors.
we are not yet ready to abandon the written word, but we do need to think about how we use it and how we can make it work harder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
academic writing teachers are in a position to play a key role in the development of students’ disciplinary writing and learning.

the role of academic writing teachers needs to change to reflect a more collaborative, dialogic approach that focuses on student learning and development, as opposed to the current emphasis on teaching and assessment.
written feedback is an important and valuable tool for academic writing teachers, but that it should be deployed strategically and with an awareness of how it might be received by students.
